DRM Model Selection: SNR and Distributional Robustness

Nested linear-regression simulation

Nested Linear model

M1:Y∼X1,M2:Y∼X1+X2+X3.M_1:Y\sim X_1, \qquad M_2:Y\sim X_1+X_2+X_3.

Y=1+β1X1+δX2+δX3(+ε).Y=1+\beta_1X_1+\delta X_2+\delta X_3(+\varepsilon).

The simulation is divided into two cases because they answer different model-selection questions.

Case 1: the simpler model M1 is true

δ=0.\delta=0.

Both models contain the true conditional mean, but the larger model contains two useless predictors. This case measures whether a selection method can prefer the simpler model when predictive distributions are very similar.

Case 2: the larger model M2 is true

δ>0.\delta>0.

The simpler model omits relevant predictors. This case measures whether a selection method detects the additional signal contained in the larger model.

Sensitivity Check

Signal-to-Noise Ratio

The total signal-to-noise ratio is

SNRtotal=Var⁡(β1X1+δX2+δX3)Var⁡(ε).\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\beta_1X_1+\delta X_2+\delta X_3)} {\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)}.

For nested model selection, the more relevant quantity in Case 2 is the discriminating SNR:

SNRdisc=Var⁡(δX2+δX3)Var⁡(ε)=2δ2.\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{disc}} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\delta X_2+\delta X_3)} {\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)}=2\delta^2.

Changing a coefficient (effect size), predictor variance, or error variance can therefore be described through SNR.

Distribution shape

Changing the distribution shape of a predictor or error term while holding its mean and variance fixed, to test the robustness of our strategy.

We generate data from 4 distribution shape with fixed mean 0 and variance 1.

distribution mean variance skewness
normal 0.0019 1.0013 0.0005
heavy_tail_t5 0.0020 0.9961 -0.0108
right_skewed -0.0031 0.9827 1.9484
contaminated_normal 0.0050 1.0159 0.0320

Research Design

We use five DRM metrics with basis function:

q(y)=(y,y2).q(y)=(y,y^2).

We also introduce AIC as a benchmark.

For each scenario, one test set (without noise) is generated before the 500 times Monte Carlo loop and remains fixed, Only the training set changes across iterations.

Representative nested scenarios

X1,X2,X3∼iidN(0,1),X_1,X_2,X_3\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1),

For each scenario, the fixed test response is noiseless. Two training responses are constructed from the same training predictors:

Ytest=1+β1X1+δX2+δX3,Y_{\mathrm{test}}=1+\beta_1X_1+\delta X_2+\delta X_3,

Ytrain,without=1+β1X1+δX2+δX3,Y_{\mathrm{train,without}}=1+\beta_1X_1+\delta X_2+\delta X_3,

Ytrain,with=1+β1X1+δX2+δX3+ε,ε∼N(0,1).Y_{\mathrm{train,with}}=1+\beta_1X_1+\delta X_2+\delta X_3+\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,1).

1. simpler model is true

Ytest=Ytrain,without=1+X1,Y_{\mathrm{test}}=Y_{\mathrm{train,without}}=1+X_1,

Ytrain,with=1+X1+ε.Y_{\mathrm{train,with}}=1+X_1+\varepsilon.

Part I: SNR experiments

Experiment 1A: the simpler model is true

Y=1+β1X1+ε,Y=1+\beta_1X_1+\varepsilon,

Both candidate models contain the true signal. The shared SNR is

SNRshared=β12σx12σϵ2.\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{shared}}=\frac{\beta_1^2 \sigma_{x_1}^2}{\sigma_\epsilon ^2}.

This finite SNR applies only to the with-noise training condition. Without-noise training has zero error variance and therefore infinite SNR; it is reported separately in the representative baseline rather than along the SNR curve.

The shared SNR was also varied by changing the predictor standard deviation or the observation-error standard deviation. These three parameterisations produced essentially the same selection pattern at matched SNR values, so the coefficient-based implementation is used in the main results for clarity.

Conclu: Increasing this quantity strengthens signal shared by both candidates; it does not increase their structural difference. DRM methods have no explicit complexity penalty, so their accuracy may remain close to chance level even when shared SNR is high.

Experiment 1B: the larger model is true

Here the larger model contains additional true signal. With unit predictor and error variances,

δ=SNRdisc/2.\delta=\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{disc}}/2}.

The zero point is excluded because it belongs to Experiment 1A, where the simpler model is true.

The same SNR equivalence applies here: changing the coefficient, predictor variance, or error variance produced essentially the same selection pattern at matched discriminating SNR values.

Conclu: When the larger model is true, models fitted to noisy training data require sufficient discriminating signal to identify the additional predictors. At low SNR, the observation error in the training response can obscure the additional signal; selection improves as the discriminating SNR increases.

The SNR curve reports only the with-noise training condition. The corresponding noiseless case is shown separately in the representative baseline.

Part II: distributional robustness

The robustness experiments are also separated by the true model. In both cases, all compared distributions have mean zero and variance one.

Concl: Overall, changing the predictor or error distribution shape does not fundamentally alter the selection pattern.

Experiment 2: changing the predictor distribution

For the simpler-true case, changing the distribution of the useless predictors examines finite-sample overfitting. For the larger-true case, the discriminating SNR is fixed at

SNRdisc=2.\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{disc}}=2.

Non-nested model

We compare two non-nested candidate models:

M1:Y∼X1vsM2:Y∼X2+X3.M_1:Y\sim X_1~~~~~~~vs \qquad M_2:Y\sim X_2+X_3.

X1,X2,X3∼iidN(0,1),ε∼N(0,1).X_1,X_2,X_3\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1), \qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,1).

M1:Y=1+β1X1+ε,SNR=β12.M_1:~~~~Y=1+\beta_1X_1+\varepsilon, \qquad \mathrm{SNR}=\beta_1^2.

M2:Y=1+δX2+δX3+ε,SNR=2δ2.M_2:~~Y=1+\delta X_2+\delta X_3+\varepsilon, \qquad \mathrm{SNR}=2\delta^2.

These finite SNR values apply only to the with-noise training condition; the noiseless condition is not included in the SNR curve.
